1	# Planetfall — Plan & Status
2	
3	_Last updated: 2026-06-10_
4	
5	## The pitch
6	
7	You're a stranded astronaut. Your ship's AI has **amnesia** — it lost all its
8	context about what happened. To escape, you explore a 3D planet, find debris,
9	and each piece hides a small puzzle solved by **recovering lost context**.
10	
11	The hook: reconstructing the ship's memory in-fiction **is the same act** as
12	recovering a real codebase's history with [Entire](https://docs.entire.io).
13	Each puzzle teaches a real `entire` command.
14	
15	> Note: `entire explain` does **not** exist (it was an early guess). The real
16	> context-recovery commands are `recap`, `checkpoint`, `activity`, `dispatch`.
17	
18	## Locked decisions
19	
20	- **3D, web-based.** Three.js + Vite, no downloaded assets — the planet is
21	  generated procedurally at load.
22	- **Planet look (approved):** a dreamy **lavender ocean world** with a few
23	  **gold metallic islands** that shimmer, wrapped in a **Saturn-style ring**.
24	  Soft, minimal, calm.
25	  - NOT earthlike. NOT the glowing-magenta-"neural"-vein look (tried it; it
26	    looked "itchy" — busy land texture fighting bright veins. Removed.)
27	  - Keep lighting (sun / ambient / env) **low** — the lavender sea washes out
28	    white if over-lit.
29	- **Build order:** get the world feeling right **first** (done), then puzzles,
30	  then the command engine + win/lose.
31	- **Two-level structure (approved 2026-06-05):** the game is two views, not one.
32	  - **Orbit view** — bird's-eye planet; click a marked **island hotspot** to land.
33	  - **Island view** — a **walkable, first-person** landscape (WASD + mouse-look);
34	    artifacts are embedded **in the terrain**, not floating on the globe. Walk up
35	    to one and press **E** to inspect; **B** leaves back to orbit.
36	  - Transition is a **crossfade cut** into a dedicated island scene (not a
37	    seamless dive onto the sphere).
38	  - Starting with **one island holding all the artifacts/puzzles**; more later.

77	## Puzzle design (PROPOSED — not yet reviewed/built)
78	
79	Arc: **orient → restore → understand → escape**. Each puzzle is small: run a
80	command → read the recovered context → use one detail from it.
81	
82	| # | Fragment | Command | What's lost | Puzzle |
83	|---|----------|-----------|-------------|--------|
84	| 1 | 🪖 EVA Helmet | `recap` | "What was I doing before the crash?" | Run `recap`; read the summary of recent log entries; pick out the mission. |
85	| 2 | 📖 Torn Logbook | `checkpoint` | A setting got corrupted in the crash | Search checkpoints, find the last good one before the corruption, rewind to it. |
86	| 3 | 🖥️ Nav Panel | `activity` | "*When* did it go wrong?" | Read the activity timeline; find when the anomaly started. |
87	| 4 | 📡 Signal Beacon | `dispatch` | No way to call for help | Generate a dispatch summarizing all recovered context, broadcast it → **win**. |
88	
89	- **#4 is the ending**: you can only send a complete dispatch after recovering
90	  the other three. This quietly answers "how do you win / how do checkpoints
91	  accumulate."
92

108	## Level 1 design — "First Memories" (agreed 2026-06-09)
109	
110	Framing inspiration: **Diner Dash**. The fun isn't the task, it's that every
111	action feeds a clear goal, each task is a short chain, a timer pushes you, and
112	you juggle toward a target. The three workflow beats map onto a Diner Dash
113	table:
114	
115	- **Do (recover/fix)** = take the order + cook
116	- **Freeze (commit)** = serve the food — locked in, but not scored yet
117	- **Checkpoint** = collect the check — *this is the step that banks progress*
118	
119	Key teaching point: in Diner Dash you can serve every table and score nothing if
120	you never collect. Same here — a frozen-but-not-checkpointed fix is a served
121	plate you never got paid for. **Freeze keeps it; checkpoint banks it.** The ship
122	rebuilds from checkpoints, not bare commits, so checkpoints literally ARE
123	forward progress.
124	
125	What a checkpoint shows (middle-ground detail — not the full real anatomy): a
126	real **12-char hex ID** (e.g. `711044b1fe29`, like real Entire checkpoints),
127	the commit **trailer** it's stamped with (`Entire-Checkpoint: <id>`), a
128	**one-line summary** of the fix, and a tiny
129	**who-did-what bar** (ship % / you %). Stands in for the real
130	transcript/prompts/token-usage/line-attribution without a spreadsheet. The ID
131	also appears stamped on the commit (ice block) so the link is visible.
132	
133	### Pressure: one level countdown (not per-memory)
134	A single **countdown clock** (top-left HUD, `TIME m:ss`) runs for the whole run
135	— tuned **scary-tight** (`TOTAL_TIME`, currently **45s** for 3 memories;
136	one-line tune in `islandView.js`). Bank every memory before it hits `0:00` or
137	the run **fails**: every un-banked memory **melts away** (sinks + fades, ice
138	included) and a "MEMORIES MELTED" screen offers **press R to try again** (full
139	reset). The clock escalates: **urgent** (red, pulsing) under 22s → **critical**
140	(frantic fast pulse + shake + glowing red digits) under 8s; it pauses while
141	you're in orbit. The **whole sky panics** too — starting at `PANIC_TIME` (22s)
142	the lavender dusk, fog, dome and sun lerp toward an angry **crimson**, eased so
143	it's barely perceptible at first and only fully reads in the last ~10s, with a
144	**throb** once critical (and held full-red behind the fail screen). One knob
145	(`PANIC_TIME` in `islandView.js`) moves the sky independently of the clock. The clock keeps running through the **final
146	`entire checkpoint list`** — that command is the real finish line, so banking
147	the last memory does NOT stop the clock; you still have to type the list before
148	`0:00` (and you can't Esc out of that final prompt). Time out there and the
149	whole run melts. This replaced the old per-memory ~14s fade — the user wanted
150	ONE clock and real pressure across the whole level, not individual items melting.
151	
152	### The loop (one memory at a time — calm tutorial, no juggling yet)
153	The player types the **real commands** into the ship's terminal (not abstract
154	keys). Walking up to a memory auto-opens an in-world command line (movement
155	freezes; keystrokes feed the terminal; Esc backs out; B returns to orbit).
156	Each step shows the exact command to type as a scaffold.
157	
158	1. A memory **surfaces** — light beam on the terrain.
159	2. Walk up → the **ship terminal opens** (`crashlog:~$`), hinting `git add`.
160	3. Type **`git add`** → memory is staged/recovered.
161	4. Type **`git commit`** → encased in **ice** (commit).
162	5. Entire then **offers to link a checkpoint** — `Link this commit to a
163	   checkpoint? [y/n]`. Press **`y`** → ice lights up, a floating real
164	   **12-char hex ID** (e.g. `711044b1fe29`) appears, the record card pops,
165	   **ship power ticks up**. (Decline with `n`
166	   and it stays an un-tracked commit — re-approach to link it later.)
167	6. Walk to the next memory.
168	7. When all are linked → **the clock is still ticking** → race to type
169	   **`entire checkpoint list`** before `0:00` to see every checkpoint you
170	   collected → ship fully restored (win). Miss it and the whole run melts.
171	
172	IMPORTANT accuracy note (user corrected this): you do NOT type `entire
173	checkpoint` to save — in real Entire, linking a checkpoint is a yes/no offer
174	made after a commit. `entire checkpoint list` is the real command, used at the
175	end to review what you've banked.
176	
177	~3 memories; tutorial scaffolds the first of each action, near-silent after.
178	Wrong commands get a "command not recognized — try: <cmd>" nudge.
179	
180	The make-it-click beats, taught via the countdown + the meter:
181	- the level **clock** is the pressure — anything not banked before `0:00` melts.
182	- `git commit` freezes it but **doesn't move the meter** — only linking the
183	  checkpoint (`y`) banks it. Teaches commit-vs-checkpoint, no "go back" mechanic.
184	
185	### Out of scope for L1 (later levels)
186	Juggling multiple memories / tighter timers; the "go back / reapply a checkpoint"
187	payoff; recap / activity / dispatch; win/lose beyond the power meter.
188	
189	## Level 2 design — "The Drone Bay" (agreed 2026-06-10, built 2026-06-10)
190	
191	**Design rule (user, 2026-06-09): one new command per level, and it must
192	visibly show the value of checkpoints.** Level 2's command is
193	**`entire checkpoint explain`**. Nothing else is new.
194	
195	After playtesting the built Archive level (below), Rizel stepped back to first
196	principles: ground each level in the day-to-day agentic workflow. The daily
197	arc is **delegate → review → accept**, and the game had no agent in it. So
198	Level 2 puts the player on the review side of delegation — the one part of
199	the loop only the human does.
200	
201	### The fiction
202	The ship is broken into **5 systems**, each a damaged work site scattered
203	across the island: ignition coils, nav core, long-range antenna, life support
204	scrubbers, landing struts. The ship gives you a **drone bay with 5 drones**
205	(one per job — no economy, no earning). Drones fix things fast, but the ship
206	won't power up work nobody can account for.
207	
208	### The loop (one countdown for the whole level)
209	1. **Assign**: walk to a broken site, press E → a drone flies out and works
210	   on it (visible work beam / sparks). You're free immediately.
211	2. **Player's choice**: babysit one drone at a time, or sprint site-to-site
212	   launching the whole fleet. Nothing forces parallelism — the clock makes it
213	   the obviously rational move (same principle as search: the tool isn't a
214	   gate, it's the rational choice). Five beams running at once while you do
215	   nothing is the level's money shot.
216	3. **Drone finishes** → the site seals under a checkpoint id. You weren't
217	   there; you don't know what it did.
218	4. **Review**: walk up to a finished site → the terminal opens **pre-filled**
219	   with `entire checkpoint explain <id>` — press Enter (no typing ids; you
220	   still SEE that real explain takes an id). A story card shows what was
221	   actually done: "replaced coolant pump · 3 attempts · 2 parts scavenged".
222	5. **Accept**: an **ADD TO SHIP** confirm appears (Y, matching L1's confirm
223	   beat) → that system comes online, ship meter +20%.
224	6. **Finish line**: the FIFTH accept keeps the terminal open — the next
225	   command happens at the prompt you're already at, like the real CLI. Type
226	   `entire dispatch` ("generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work" —
227	   five drones just worked; the report writes itself from the checkpoints).
228	   `entire checkpoint list` still works there as an optional L1 callback and
229	   nudges you to dispatch. (Changed 2026-06-10 from "walk back to the console
230	   and run `list`" — Rizel couldn't find the console at the end; a final
231	   fetch-quest was friction, not tension, and dispatch is the truer end-of-day
232	   command. If the player wanders off, any online system or the bay console
233	   reopens the report prompt.)
234	
235	Fail = clock hits 0:00 before all five are accepted → R to retry.
236	
237	### Deliberately NOT in Level 2
238	No bad/botched drone work (no deduction, nothing to compare — explain is the
239	gate to the ADD TO SHIP button, not a puzzle), no drone management or upgrade
240	mechanics (more drones = parallelism, never new mechanics), no typing
241	checkpoint ids, no values to extract from explanations. The "one drone did it
242	wrong — find it" twist is reserved as a possible later level once this loop
243	is proven.
244	
245	### The upgrade table (drones don't repair — they IMPROVISE)
246	The transformation is what makes you *need* the explanation: you left a bent
247	dish, you come back to a lance pointed at the sky — "what did you DO?" is the
248	urge `explain` exists to satisfy.
249	
250	| System (broken) | Becomes | Explain card flavor |
251	|---|---|---|
252	| Ignition coils (charred leaning stack) | **Plasma Ring** — floating gold torus | "coils beyond saving — rebuilt as a plasma ring from salvaged hull plate · 2 attempts" |
253	| Nav core (cracked dark gyro) | **Star Dome** — projected starfield + orbiting ring | "core unrecoverable — remapped from scratch; starfield calibrated to the lavender belt" |
254	| Long-range antenna (dish face-down in the dirt) | **Signal Spire** — lance firing a beam to orbit | "dish unsalvageable — respun the mast into a spire · 3 attempts · the first two fell over" |
255	| Life support scrubbers (rusty vent box) | **Garden Pod** — glass dome, glowing plants | "filters dead — replaced with a living filter; two vines scavenged from the crash" |
256	| Landing struts (collapsed leg) | **Grav Skid** — hover pad bobbing over a glow ring | "strut seized solid — swapped for grav skids; technically the ship floats now" |
257	
258	Visual grammar (status readable from across the island via beam color):
259	amber beam = broken (blinking red warn bulb up close) → cyan pulsing beam +
260	hovering drone + work beam = drone at work → ice-blue beam + L1-style ice
261	seal + floating checkpoint id = finished, review me → no beam = accepted
262	(the upgrade itself is the landmark; ice melts, animations wake up).
263	
264	### The teaching, felt not told
265	What the level actually shows (Rizel's framing, 2026-06-10 — keep it this
266	way): **you can have multiple agents working in parallel, see what work each
267	one did, and get a summary at the end.** Sending a drone (E) is one button —
268	delegation is demonstrated as spectacle, not taught; ADD TO SHIP is just the
269	gate that makes reading the explanation non-skippable. The two things the
270	player genuinely learns are the commands: `entire checkpoint explain` (see
271	what an agent did while you weren't watching — the level's one taught
272	mechanic) and `entire dispatch` (the day, summarized — a ceremonial closer
273	with nothing to learn, the role `list` played in L1). Arc: L1 — bank it.
274	L2 — agents work, you can always see and summarize what they did.
275	Search/rewind/recap reserved for later levels, by which point the checkpoint
276	history will have grown naturally.
277	
278	### Implementation (2026-06-10)
279	Lives in `src/droneBayView.js`; HUD block `#db-hud` in `index.html`; styles
280	share L1's countdown/briefing/fail selectors. The shelved Archive level stays
281	fully playable at `?view=archive`; `?view=level2` / `?level=2` and the
282	post-L1 glitching pin now route to the Drone Bay. Specifics:
283	- 5 sites + 5 parked drones by the console (bay row at z=50, heights
284	  node-verified). Drones arc to the site (~26 u/s), hover-orbit while
285	  working (`WORK_TIME` 18s), then fly home. Work continues while the player
286	  is elsewhere — that's the point.
287	- One 150s clock (`TOTAL_TIME`); serial play (~35s/system × 5) can't beat it,
288	  the fleet can. Same panic-sky as L1.
289	- Fleet status panel (top-left): BROKEN / DRONE AT WORK / READY TO REVIEW /
290	  ONLINE per system.
291	- Review terminal auto-opens at a sealed site, pre-filled with
292	  `entire checkpoint explain <id>` — Enter runs it (no id typing), card rows
293	  print, then a green **ADD TO SHIP** button (clickable; Y also works).
294	- Finish line: the fifth accept rolls the same terminal into report mode;
295	  typed `entire dispatch` prints the day report (5 upgrades, "crew: 1 human,
296	  5 drones"), then the win screen. `entire checkpoint list` optional there.
297	- Fail at 0:00 → R resets everything (sites, drones, clock).
298	- Bird's-eye map (M, `src/overhead.js`) on all island levels — top-down
299	  camera + you-are-here arrow, walking still works, terminals open over it.

301	## Level 3 design — "Launch Clearance" (agreed + built 2026-06-10 — name TBD, pending playtest)
302	
303	The final level. Designed across two sessions on 2026-06-10 (the morning
304	session's "anomaly squashing" draft evolved into this; rejected on the way:
305	"The Other Ship" dead-crew mystery — "good story but far too many details",
306	raw search box-checking — "eh", and symptom-matching — "how would they know").
307	Simplicity bar (Rizel): GitHub's Bug Bash — "all they do is squash bugs and
308	pick up lifepoints. simplicity."
309	
310	**The aha to deliver** (modeled on a real moment: Claude answered "what were
311	the level 3 plans?" from this repo's own checkpoint transcripts): you're asked
312	a question you provably can't answer from memory, and the record answers it.
313	L2 already manufactured the situation — the subagents worked while you weren't
314	watching. **Arc: L1 — bank your work. L2 — subagents work while you don't
315	watch. L3 — someone asks about that work; you weren't there, the record was.**
316	
317	### The fiction
318	The ship is repaired — now it has to fly. The player is **inside the ship,
319	in the pilot's chair** (first time aboard; alone signals "finale"). The launch
320	computer won't arm on work nobody can account for — the same rule the ship
321	enforced in L2, escalated to takeoff. The questioner is the **ship's AI: the
322	amnesiac from Level 1**, verifying against the memory the player banked for
323	it. First scene and last scene are the same character, before and after.
324	Briefing line (approved verbatim, keep it):
325	
326	> "I can read the record. Protocol says you have to be the one to confirm it."
327	
328	### The loop (whole level at one console — no walking)
329	~5 questions under one clock, constant shape, two clicks each:
330	1. A question appears in plain words — answerable **only from the record**:
331	   "The antenna repair — how many attempts did it take?"
332	2. The terminal offers **~3 tools as multiple choice** (click / number key) —
333	   e.g. `entire checkpoint explain <id>` / Skill: *what-happened* /
334	   `entire dispatch`.
335	3. It runs **visibly**, answering in that tool's voice: raw command → the full
336	   record card; a skill → visibly runs the command, then one plain sentence
337	   (the skills pitch, demonstrated not explained).
338	4. **Answer chips** ([2] [3] [5]) — the answer is on screen in the output.
339	   Zero typing, zero keyword guessing, zero memory.
340	5. Correct → a **launch-code segment locks** (▣ ▣ □ □ □), the system audibly
341	   arms in the cabin, the matching upgrade flares out on the island. Wrong →
342	   the card stays up, the clock keeps eating, click again.
343	6. 5/5 → code complete → countdown → **liftoff = the game's ending** (planet
344	   falls away, the labeled upgrades shrinking below). Win screen carries
345	   `npx skills add https://github.com/entireio/skills`.
346	
347	Fail = launch window missed at 0:00 → R to retry.
348	
349	### Tool-menu rules (Rizel's locked preferences)
350	- **Mostly ALL VALID, occasional dead end.** Usually 2 of 3 options genuinely
351	  answer it in different voices; one is a polite dead end that prints
352	  real-but-unhelpful output and costs only clock seconds (e.g. picking
353	  `explain` when you don't know *which* checkpoint — the fizzle teaches the
354	  search-vs-explain boundary). Never a fail state at the menu.
355	- **Menus ROTATE by question type** (never the same trio twice): what
356	  happened at one site → `explain` / Skill: *what-happened*; don't-know-where
357	  → `search` (the keyword comes from the question, never guessed — redeems
358	  the shelved Archive); order/when → `list` / `activity`; handoff flavor →
359	  Skill: *session-handoff* / *teach*; finale → `dispatch` (ceremonial closer,
360	  maybe no menu at all).
361	- **Small cast:** ~2–3 skills + 3–4 commands across the whole level — "we
362	  dont have to use every skill"; 11 skills would be a product tour.
363	- Possible easing: auto-run the tool on Q1–2, introduce the menu on Q3–5.
364	
365	### Deliberately NOT in Level 3
366	No typed search words, no free-text answers, no remembering things seen once
367	(every answer is on screen at the moment of choice), no fault-finding/blame
368	mechanic, no new mechanics past the two-click beat. Skills repo lives at
369	`~/Documents/work/skills` (11 skills) — only a few appear.
370	
371	### Open knobs (decide at build/playtest)
372	- Level name ("Launch Clearance" is a placeholder).
373	- Question count (~5) and which question types make the cut.
374	- The "discrepancy" question — one answer that surprises the player (grav
375	  skids: "torque spec: vibes") — safe cousin of the reserved "one drone did
376	  it wrong" twist. In or out?
377	- Trade-off to playtest: this is the least game-bodied level (terminal +
378	  cabin, island as backdrop) — fits the operator→delegator graduation, but
379	  compare against a variant with one short walk per question if it feels flat
380	  after the Drone Bay.
381	- How the cabin/console is staged in 3D (new interior view vs. dressed-up
382	  terminal overlay).
383	
384	### Implementation (2026-06-10)
385	Lives in `src/launchView.js`; HUD block `#lc-hud` in `index.html`; styles
386	share the countdown/briefing/win/fail selector groups. `?view=level3` /
387	`?level=3` dev shortcut; L2's `entire dispatch` (onComplete) opens the launch
388	window — the orbit pin then boards the ship. Build decisions on the knobs:
389	- **Staging:** fixed cockpit rig above the bay (eye height 19, node-verified
390	  sightlines to all five upgrades), simple slab window frame + glowing dash
391	  glued to the camera, idle sway. The L2 upgrades stand on the island, alive
392	  (exported `SYSTEMS` + `UPGRADE_BUILDERS` from droneBayView).
393	- **5 questions:** antenna attempts (explain / what-happened / dispatch dead
394	  end), hull plate (search / recall / explain dead end), record count (list /
395	  recall / search dead end), why-the-ship-floats — the discrepancy question
396	  IS in (explain / what-happened / list dead end), then `entire dispatch`
397	  files the flight log (single pre-filled Enter, ceremonial).
398	- Confirm → gold beam flare at that system + a launch-code segment locks
399	  (shows the checkpoint's first hex). Wrong chip: dimmed, clock keeps eating.
400	  Dead-end tool: output prints, option struck through, try another.
401	- Liftoff: ~9s climb-out — island falls away, sky lerps to space, stars fade
402	  in — then the LIFTOFF win screen with the `npx skills add` line.
403	- One 150s window (`TOTAL_TIME`), same low/critical/panic-sky grammar as
404	  L1/L2; fail = LAUNCH WINDOW MISSED → R resets everything.

406	## Level ? design — "The Archive" (built 2026-06-09, SHELVED for a later level)
407	
408	Built as Level 2, then shelved 2026-06-10 after a playtest: the story carried
409	too much weight ("meh, it just feels like too much") and search is a
410	weeks-later pain, not a day-to-day one. The implementation is kept intact in
411	`src/archiveView.js`, playable at `?view=archive` — it should return as a
412	later search level, by which point the player's checkpoint history (incl.
413	drone work) will have grown enough that search needs no lore-dump. Its
414	command was **`entire checkpoint search`**.
415	
416	Rejected on the way here (kept for the record so we don't re-tread):
417	- An elaborate "corruption" level teaching search + explain + rewind with
418	  clue-hunting, decoy checkpoints, and a spreading corruption zone — **too many
419	  variables to consume at once**.
420	- `rewind` as the L2 command — in the simple framings it kept mis-modeling the
421	  tool (reading as "restore from backup" when real rewind means "take my
422	  *current* state back to a save point; the bank itself is never at risk").
423	- `recap` — L1's three collected items don't warrant a recap; manufacturing the
424	  need (more items, mixed states, a blackout) was creeping back toward
425	  variable-overload.
426	
427	### The fiction
428	Level 1's win restored the ship's memory — side effect: the ship's **entire
429	pre-crash checkpoint archive surfaces**. The island is now dotted with ~20
430	identical dark frozen memories (ice blocks, no beams, unreadable from a
431	distance). Most were never grabbed by the player — the corpus is deliberately
432	**bigger than your head**, because that's the situation search exists for.
433	The player's 3 L1 checkpoints can appear in the archive as a continuity touch.
434	
435	### The loop (×3, one countdown clock for tension)
436	1. **The ship asks** for a memory in a plain sentence that contains the
437	   keyword: *"I need the memory of the **ignition sequence**."* (No clue
438	   hunting — the search word is right there in the request.)
439	2. **Player types** `entire checkpoint search "ignition"` at the terminal.
440	3. **The matching block's beam lights up** across the island — the money shot:
441	   a dark field, one typed word, one light. (In L1 the game lit the beams for
442	   you; in L2 nothing lights until YOU search.)
443	4. **Sprint over, press E** → memory transmits to the ship, power meter
444	   climbs, next request.
445	
446	Wrong/misspelled word → 0 results, no penalty except the ticking clock (which
447	is exactly the real-world cost of bad search terms). Searching by walking the
448	field and inspecting blocks one-by-one stays *possible* but ruinously slow —
449	the tool isn't a gate, it's the obviously rational move.
450	
451	The teaching, felt not told: **your history quickly outgrows your memory;
452	you remember a *word*, not a place — search turns the word into the moment.**
453	Arc so far: L1 — bank it. L2 — search it. (recap / dispatch / resume / rewind
454	reserved for later levels.)
455	
456	### Deliberately NOT in Level 2
457	No clue collection, no decoy results, no timestamps, no `explain`, no rewind
458	browser, no new artifact states. The ~20 archive blocks are set dressing, not
459	state to track. Retrieval is a plain E-grab — the level's typing effort lives
460	in the search command itself (leaning: keep it that simple rather than rerun
461	L1's add/commit beat per item; revisit after a playtest).
462	
463	### Implementation (2026-06-09)
464	Lives in `src/archiveView.js` (the abandoned corruption level was stripped;
465	kept from that work: `src/memoryProps.js`, the `onComplete` hook in
466	`islandView.js`, the `#fp-shared` HUD split, the glitching-pin entry after L1
467	completes, and the `?view=level2` / `?level=2` dev shortcuts). Specifics:
468	- **21 archive blocks** (3 targets + 15 old-crew checkpoints + the 3 L1
469	  recoveries with the dev-scaffold ids), scattered deterministically on dry
470	  land (seeded RNG, min spacing, never in the sea or on the console).
471	- Blocks are dark and anonymous; an id sprite appears only when lit, grabbed,
472	  or walked up close (~18u) — browsing on foot stays possible but slow.
473	- The ship's request panel (top-left, under the clock) holds the keyword in a
474	  plain sentence. Terminal (gold beam, auto-opens like L1) accepts
475	  `entire checkpoint search "<word>"` and `entire checkpoint list` (prints all
476	  21 — "too many to read" — the why-search-exists beat).
477	- Search lights every match's cyan beam (previous search goes dark); E on the
478	  requested block transmits it (warm gold); E on a lit-but-wrong block costs
479	  only the re-read. 0 results cost only clock.
480	- One 90s countdown (tunable `TOTAL_TIME`), same panic-sky as L1, fail = R to
481	  retry, win = "ARCHIVE LINKED" + B to orbit.
482	
483	## Title screen (built 2026-06-11)
484	
485	Borrowed from Mona's Bug Bash (bug-bash.github.com — Rizel's simplicity bar):
486	the game boots to an arcade menu over the live orbit view (the planet is the
487	attract backdrop). START GAME / OPTIONS; Options holds CONTROLS (the full
488	key list, all three levels) and SOUND (music ON/OFF + volume — driven through
489	the existing #audio-panel controls so the two can never disagree). ↑/↓ +
490	Enter / Esc-back navigation with a ▸ cursor; mouse hover/click also works.
491	Lives in `src/titleScreen.js` + `#title-screen` in `index.html`; shown only on
492	a clean boot — `?view=` / `?level=` dev shortcuts skip it. While it's up, a
493	`body.title-up` class hides the in-game chrome (small logo, hint, audio
494	panel, pin). A nice side effect: the first menu interaction is the user
495	gesture that unblocks music autoplay — the "press start" beat is real.
496	
497	### Story intro (added 2026-06-11, story agreed with Rizel the same day)
498	START GAME plays 5 narrator beats in a Bug Bash-style box over the planet
499	(Space/Enter/click advance, Esc skips, last beat cues "BEGIN"), then drops
500	into orbit. The story (`STORY_BEATS` in titleScreen.js): the old world saved
501	every line of code but was made for humans only — no space for everyone now
502	that humans and AI agents build together — so you left for a new world in
503	your own spaceship with your five subagent friends; the ship broke down and
504	crashed, and the pieces that keep it running scattered across an island;
505	bring the pieces back, wake your friends, fix the ship, fly again.
506	
507	Story rules agreed with Rizel (keep these):
508	- **Unnamed storybook narrator** (the Bug Bash voice) — nobody in-fiction
509	  narrates. NO "ship's AI" as a character; the L3 questioner is just the
510	  launch computer doing what launch computers do.
511	- **The player's memory is fine.** "You weren't there — your checkpoints
512	  were" requires it; amnesia would weaken the pitch. The crash scattered the
513	  ship's parts (L1 reveals they're its memory) — nothing was "wiped".
514	- **The old world is outgrown, never bad** — a size problem ("not enough
515	  space for everyone"), not a feature gap. Never name any real-world tool.
516	- **Plain language for non-native speakers**: short sentences, common words,
517	  no idioms or sci-fi jargon ("the jump went wrong" was rejected). Pending:
518	  the same pass over the level briefings; "bank" is load-bearing teaching
519	  vocabulary — keep it but introduce it gently.
520	- The player is a fan of agent-human collaboration; the L2 drones are "your
521	  five subagent friends" who crashed with you (briefing copy not yet
522	  re-tinted — pending).
523	
524	### The TV look (decided 2026-06-12)
525	Scanlines + vignette over the whole screen, **on by default**, toggled at
526	Options > Display > TV EFFECT (remembered in localStorage, key
527	`pf-tv-effect`). Pure CSS overlay (`#tv-overlay`, body class `tv-on`),
528	pointer-events off, game plays identically. Tried and REJECTED on the way
529	(2026-06-12, don't re-tread): the Bug Bash-style inset screen / bezel border
530	("i dont think i like the border"), an RGB aperture-grille layer (invisible
531	at distance, just dims), and a rolling bright band (competes with the
532	countdown/panic-sky urgency signals during play). This is the one permanent
533	texture allowed over the flat look — a film-grain decision, not a graphics
534	overhaul; nothing else gets layered on without asking.
535	
536	Still on the Bug Bash-inspired list (discussed 2026-06-11, not yet built):
537	ship-AI-free narrator beats replacing the briefing walls (one goal sentence +
538	one controls line, Space to advance).
539	
540	## Architecture / where things live
541	
542	```
543	index.html         # canvas + HUD + crossfade overlay + FP prompt + panel + loader
544	src/style.css      # HUD / panel / loader / fade / crosshair / FP-prompt styling
545	src/main.js        # VIEW MANAGER: owns renderer + resize + shared panel + the
546	                   #   render loop; crossfades between the two views.
547	                   #   ?view=island jumps straight onto the island (dev aid).
548	src/titleScreen.js # arcade boot menu (START GAME / OPTIONS > controls, sound)
549	                   #   over the orbit view; clean boots only, dev URLs skip it.
550	src/planetView.js  # orbit view: scene/lighting/stars/planet/clouds/atmo/ring +
551	                   #   the clickable gold landing hotspot. onIslandClick callback.
552	src/islandView.js  # LEVEL 1: sky/light, terrain+water, the memories, terminal
553	                   #   loop, countdown. enter()/exit()/onExit/onComplete.
554	src/droneBayView.js# LEVEL 2 ("The Drone Bay"): 5 broken systems, 5 drones,
555	                   #   pre-filled `entire checkpoint explain` + ADD TO SHIP.
556	                   #   Exports SYSTEMS + UPGRADE_BUILDERS for Level 3.
557	src/launchView.js  # LEVEL 3 ("Launch Clearance"): cockpit finale at one
558	                   #   console — ship AI asks, pick the tool (1/2/3), confirm
559	                   #   the answer, launch code fills, liftoff = the ending.
560	src/archiveView.js # SHELVED search level ("The Archive"), at ?view=archive:
561	                   #   ~21 dark blocks, ship requests, checkpoint search beat.
562	src/memoryProps.js # shared props: beam texture, ice block, id sprite, id gen
563	src/overhead.js    # bird's-eye map toggle (M) for all island levels: fixed
564	                   #   top-down camera + gold you-are-here arrow; walking
565	                   #   still works while overhead (fp alwaysMove flag)
566	src/terrain.js     # procedural island heightmap mesh + water + heightAt(x,z)
567	src/firstPerson.js # PointerLockControls + WASD walker, glued to the terrain
568	src/noise.js       # seedable 3D simplex + fBm (sphere-sampled → seamless)
569	src/planet.js      # bakes planet maps; createElevationSampler() finds land for
570	                   #   the hotspot. Palette constants (DEEP/SHALLOW/SNOW) here.
571	src/atmosphere.js  # fresnel limb-glow shell shader (orbit view)
572	src/ring.js        # procedural banded ring (radial-remapped UVs)
573	src/debris.js      # FRAGMENTS[] (lore + command) + exported prop BUILDERS,
574	                   #   reused as the island artifacts. createDebris() is now
575	                   #   unused (kept for reference / git history).
576	```
577	
578	Run: `npm install` then `npm run dev` → http://localhost:5173
579	Controls: orbit = drag/scroll, click the gold marker to land. Island = click to
580	capture mouse, WASD to walk, E to inspect a glowing artifact, B to leave.
581	
582	## History
583	Repo started as `signalkit` (a Python telemetry CLI), then pivoted to Planetfall
584	on 2026-06-05. The old code is recoverable via git history + Entire checkpoints.
585	
```

I've got the full picture. Here's where the project stands.

## Planetfall — what it is

A **3D browser game** (Three.js + Vite) that teaches real `entire` CLI commands through fiction. You're a crash-landed traveler who left the "old world" (built for humans-only code) for a new planet with your **five subagent friends**. The ship crashed, its parts scattered across an island — recovering them *is* the act of recovering a codebase's history with Entire.

It pivoted from a Python telemetry CLI (`signalkit`) to this game on 2026-06-05.

## The game is feature-complete across all 3 levels

| Level | Name | Teaches | Loop |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L1** | First Memories | `git add`/`commit` + checkpoint linking (`y/n`), `entire checkpoint list` | Diner Dash beat — *freeze keeps it, checkpoint banks it*; one tight countdown |
| **L2** | The Drone Bay | `entire checkpoint explain` + `entire dispatch` | 5 drones improvise repairs in parallel; review each, ADD TO SHIP |
| **L3** | Launch Clearance | pick-the-tool multiple choice (explain/search/list/skills) | Cockpit finale — answer questions only the *record* can answer → liftoff = ending |

Plus a shelved **Archive** search level (`?view=archive`), an **arcade title screen**, and a **bird's-eye map** (M).

## Where we *actually* left off — uncommitted WIP

Last commit was the title screen (2026-06-11). Since then there's **uncommitted work that's complete and coherent but not yet committed**, all on the title screen / presentation layer:

2. **The TV look** (2026-06-12) — scanlines + vignette CSS overlay, on by default, toggled at **Options › Display › TV EFFECT** (remembered in localStorage). The one permanent texture allowed over the flat look.

These touch `titleScreen.js`, `index.html`, `style.css`, `README.md`, and `PLAN.md` — and they're already documented in PLAN.md, so the docs and code are in sync. The `.codex/` dir (agents + hooks.json) is untracked but unrelated.

> AGENT

Confirmed the root cause. At boot, `planetView.enter()` frames the island front-and-center — but then the planet keeps spinning at `0.02 rad/s` through the *entire* title menu + 5-beat story (easily 30–60s). By the time the story ends, the island has drifted far to the side (or the pin's hidden), and you wait for it to swing back.

The title screen passes **no `onStart` callback** (`main.js:141`), so nothing re-frames the orbit when the story ends — the title just fades away over the already-drifted planet.

Fix: re-frame the island the moment the story finishes. I'll extract the framing into a reusable `reframe()` (calling `enter()` again would double-bind the pointer listeners), then wire it to `onStart`.

> TOOL

Called on enter, and\n  // again when the story ends — the planet drifts the whole time the title +\n  // story are up, so without this the island has rotated away by the time you\n  // arrive in orbit.\n  function reframe() {\n    scene.updateMatrixWorld(true);\n    anchor.getWorldPosition(tmpWorld);\n    const dir = tmpWorld.clone().normalize();\n    camera.position.copy(dir).multiplyScalar(6.4);\n    camera.position.y += 0.7; // tip the island slightly below centre\n    controls.target.set(0, 0, 0);\n    controls.update();\n  }\n\n  function enter() {\n    active = true;\n    reframe();\n\n    canvas.addEventListener(\"pointermove\", onPointerMove);"

Done. Here's the behavior now:

- The planet keeps gently auto-rotating throughout (unchanged — `update()` still drifts it at `0.02 rad/s`).
- The instant the story finishes (last beat → "BEGIN", or Esc-skip), `planetView.reframe()` swings the camera so the landing-site island is **front-and-center and clickable**. The hard camera move happens behind the title's 0.6s fade-out, so you don't see it jump.
- After that, the planet continues drifting slowly — so it's "still moving but in your view," exactly what you described.

A subtle bonus: `reframe()` is shared by `enter()` too, so I didn't duplicate the framing logic or risk double-binding the pointer listeners.

> AGENT

Honest answer: I didn't pick it for the story bar — I **reused the game's existing UI palette**, which is defined once in `:root` (`src/style.css:1-4`):

- `--accent: #6fe3ff` — the light blue/cyan
- `--accent-warm: #ffb86b` — the orange/gold
- `--ink: #e8f4ff` — near-white text
- plus the dark navy backgrounds

That cyan-on-navy-with-gold scheme is the convention across **all** the in-game chrome — the terminals, the HUD, the briefings, the panels. So when I built the story bar I leaned on the same variables to keep it consistent with everything else.

But it's worth flagging a real tension you may be reacting to: **the world and the chrome don't match.** Your locked planet look is a *"dreamy lavender ocean world with gold metallic islands"* (PLAN.md). So the 3D scene is **lavender + gold**, while the UI on top of it is **cyan + gold**. The cyan is a holdover sci-fi-HUD default, not something derived from your approved palette. That mismatch is probably what reads as "why are we doing this."

If you want, I could retune the chrome toward the world — swap the cyan accent for a **lavender/violet** that matches the ocean, keeping the gold as the warm accent. That's a one-line change to `--accent` that would ripple through everything consistently. Want me to try that (I can scope it to just the story bar first so you can compare before committing to a global swap)?

Here's the story bar in four palettes, each over a lavender+gold world backdrop so you can judge them against the actual scene:

1. **Current (cyan + gold)** — the cyan top edge reads cool/techy and is the one color *not* in your world; it slightly fights the lavender.
2. **Lavender + gold** — the accent is pulled from the ocean itself, gold cue from the islands. Ties into the world; warmest fit.
3. **Warm / gold-forward** — drops cyan entirely, goes sepia-ish. Cozy but reads a bit brown/muddy against the lavender.
4. **Minimal (white, no accent)** — neutral white line + text, lets the world supply all the color. Closest to a clean storybook/Bug-Bash dialogue card.

My honest take: **#2 or #4**. #2 if you want the chrome to feel part of the world; #4 if you want the bar to get out of the way and let the planet be the color. #1 (what we have) and #3 are the weakest here.

> AGENT

Totally get it — the current text *explains* the world, it never *talks to you* or *asks you for anything*. That's the whole gap. A game opening works because someone (or something) turns to the player and says: *here's the situation, here's what's at stake, I need you to go do this thing.* Let me give you ways to get that feeling — including the "rebellion" angle and how to keep it from turning into humans-vs-agents.

## First: who's doing the talking?

You said you don't have an NPC. You actually have three candidates already in the fiction — any of them gives you a "someone is addressing you" voice:

- **Your five agent friends.** They're your crew. They can talk to you in the intro — banter, excitement about the trip — *and then go silent in the crash.* Now the through-line has a face: "wake your friends" stops being a task and becomes *getting your friends back.* Strong emotional hook, and you already planned them as characters.
- **A call from the new world.** A short transmission *inviting/recruiting* you — "we're building a place for all of us, come help, come live free." That's the voice that gives you a mission *and* a destination worth crashing on the way to. (This is your "rebellion" instinct, made warm.)
- **Mission-control / second-person narrator that briefs you.** Not a character exactly, but the narrator stops describing and starts *tasking*: "You weren't supposed to land here. But here's what you do now." Closest to your current setup, smallest change.

My pick: **your agent friends open it, the new world's call is what you were answering.** Both at once — crew gives heart, the call gives purpose.

## Second: the shape of a mission opening (call to adventure)

Almost every game intro is the same five beats. Yours can be too:

1. **The good thing** — you + your agents build together, and it's great. (one warm beat)
2. **The problem / the call** — the old place can't hold all of you; somewhere out there, people are building a world that can, and they're calling for builders. *You said yes.* (this is the "why am I playing")
3. **The turn** — "Oh no." The crash.
4. **The stakes** — ship in pieces, friends gone quiet, you're stranded short of the place you were trying to reach.
5. **The mission, said to you** — "Get the ship's memory back. Wake your friends. Finish the trip." ← the player now knows exactly why they're here.

Right now your text nails 1 and 2 but spends *all* its energy there and rushes 3–5 — so the player gets a lecture, not a mission.

## Third: the "rebellion" without race wars

Your worry is right, and there's a clean fix: **make the cause about *building something new*, not *fighting someone old.*** Pioneers, not soldiers.

- The enemy isn't humans. The "antagonist" is a *limit* — the old world simply has **no more room**, and it was built back when people worked alone, so there's nowhere to bring your agents. You're not rebelling *against* people; you're **leaving to build a place where you don't have to choose.** Frontier story, founding story — the appeal of "the rebellion" (purpose, belonging, a cause worth the risk) without an out-group.
- Words that carry the cause-energy safely: *the new world, the settlement, the frontier, the build, the ones who said yes, room for everyone.* Words to avoid: *war, enemy, them, take back, fight.*
- If you want a *little* edge, aim it at the situation, not a group: the trip is dangerous, the frontier is unproven, the crash is the universe testing whether you meant it. Stakes from risk, not from villains.

## A taste, so you can feel it

Here's beat 2 (the call/mission) in each voice, just to compare flavors — not final, just to react to:

- **Crew voice:** *"Almost there!" one of your agents says. "A whole world being built for people and agents — and they want us in it."*
- **The call:** *"To anyone still out there: we're building a world with room for all of you. Bring your agents. Come help. Come home."*
- **Mission-narrator:** *"You'd heard the call — a new world, built for people and agents both. So you packed the ship, gathered your five friends, and went."*

---

---

## Entire CLI - Game Narrative Research Report

Based on my read-only exploration of the codebase, here's the grounded vocabulary and concepts from the real Entire tool:

---

### 1. **Core Concept / Pitch**

**From the README (line 3-10):**
> "Entire hooks into your Git workflow to capture AI agent sessions as you work. Sessions are indexed alongside commits, creating a searchable record of how code was written in your repo."

**One-liner:** Entire creates a permanent, searchable record of AI-driven code work by capturing agent sessions and linking them to git commits.

---

### 2. **Key Vocabulary & Real Terms**

Here are the exact nouns Entire uses, pulled from code and docs:

| Term | Definition / Context |
|------|---------------------|
| **Session** | "A complete interaction with your AI agent, from start to finish. Each session captures all prompts, responses, files modified, and timestamps." Format: `YYYY-MM-DD-<UUID>` e.g., `2026-01-08-abc123de-f456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890` |
| **Checkpoint** | "A snapshot within a session that you can rewind to—a 'save point' in your work." Created when you or the agent make a git commit. Format: 12-character hex string (e.g., `a3b2c4d5e6f7`). |
| **Transcript** | The raw agent conversation/work log. Format is agent-specific: JSONL for Claude Code/Cursor/Codex, JSON for Gemini. Stored in session metadata. Can be streamed via `entire session info <id> --transcript`. |
| **Metadata** | Session-specific data (prompts, token usage, files touched). Stored on `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Sharded by checkpoint ID. |
| **Shadow branch** | Temporary git branch (`entire/<commit[:7]>-<worktreeHash[:6]>`) that holds full worktree snapshots + metadata before condensation to permanent branch. |
| **Entire-Checkpoint trailer** | Git commit trailer (`Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7`) that links user commits to checkpoint metadata. Added automatically by post-commit hook. |
| **Recap** | "Summarize recent checkpoint activity" — displays aggregated activity with time ranges (day/week/month/90d), agent breakdown, team view. |
| **Dispatch** | "Generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work" — creates a narrative summary of recent commits/sessions with optional voice/tone, searchable across branches. |
| **Activity** | "Show your activity overview" — personal contribution stats (throughput, iteration, streak, hourly heatmap) with recent commits listed. |
| **Explain** | "Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints." Show what happened during agent-driven development, with optional AI-generated summaries. |
| **Attach** | Re-connect to a detached agent session (e.g., after terminal crash). `entire session attach <session-id>`. |
| **Resume** | "Switch to a branch, restore latest checkpointed session metadata, and show command(s)" — restore agent state from a previous branch. `entire session resume <branch>`. |
| **Token usage** | Tracked per session/checkpoint. Fields: `InputTokens`, `OutputTokens`, `CacheReadTokens`, `CacheCreationTokens`, `APICallCount`. Displayed in human form (e.g., "12.3k tokens"). |
| **Worktree** | Git worktree (concurrent working directory). Entire tracks sessions per worktree independently. |
| **Files touched** | The list of files modified during a session/checkpoint. Stored in session metadata. |
| **Entire-managed branch** | The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch (and optional `refs/entire/checkpoints/v1.1` mirror) that stores all checkpoint metadata separately from user code. |

**Notably missing from real Entire:**
- No "memory" or "context" terminology — sessions and transcripts are the units.
- No "dispatch" as a technical component — it's a command that *generates* summaries.
- No generic "event" or "activity log" — these are emergent from sessions + checkpoints.

---

### 3. **What is a "checkpoint" — What It Links/Records**

**A checkpoint is a bidirectional link between user commits and session metadata:**

1. **User-side (git commit):**
   - A trailer `Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7` is added to the commit message by the `prepare-commit-msg` hook
   - The checkpoint ID is a stable 12-hex identifier

2. **Metadata-side (entire/checkpoints/v1 branch):**
   - Sharded directory structure: `<checkpoint-id[:2]>/<checkpoint-id[2:]>/`
   - Root-level `metadata.json` (aggregated stats)
   - Per-session subdirectories (`0/`, `1/`, etc.) containing:
     - `metadata.json` (session-specific: prompts, timestamps, token counts, files touched)
     - `full.jsonl` (raw transcript from agent)
     - `prompt.txt` (user prompts scoped to this checkpoint)
     - `content_hash.txt`

3. **What it records (from `WriteCommittedOptions`):**
   - `CheckpointID`, `SessionID`
   - `Transcript` (bytes — the full agent conversation)
   - `Prompts` (list of user-submitted prompts)
   - `Context` (context window)
   - `FilesTouched` (list)
   - `TokenUsage` (input/output/cache tokens, API call count)
   - `Branch` (which branch it was committed to)
   - Strategy used

**It does NOT store:**
- The actual code changes (those stay in git commits)
- Agent decisions/reasoning (captured in transcript only)

**From README (line 187-191):**
> "Checkpoints are saved as you work. When you commit, session metadata is permanently stored on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch and linked to your commit."

---

### 4. **Session History / Recovery**

Yes, there is a real concept of exploring agent work history. Commands that surface it:

| Command | What It Does |
|---------|-------------|
| `entire session list` | "List all sessions tracked by Entire, including ended sessions." Shows SessionID, agent, model, started time, turns, checkpoints, token usage, last prompt. |
| `entire session info <session-id>` | "Display detailed state for a session." Shows agent, model, status, worktree, timing, token usage, checkpoint linkage, files touched. Three output modes: text (human), `--json` (metadata), `--transcript` (raw agent bytes). |
| `entire session current` | "Show the active session for the current worktree." Scoped to your machine/worktree. |
| `entire session attach <session-id>` | "Attach an existing agent session" — reconnect to a session (e.g., after terminal loss). |
| `entire session resume <branch>` | "Switch to a branch and resume its session." Restores latest session metadata + prints command to continue. |
| `entire checkpoint list` | "List checkpoints on the current branch." Can filter by session with `--session <id>`. |
| `entire checkpoint explain <id\|sha>` | "Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints." Shows what happened, with optional AI-generated summary. |
| `entire activity` | "Display your activity overview, repository breakdown, and recent commits from entire.io" — shows your personal stats and recent work. |
| `entire recap` | "Summarize recent checkpoint activity" — team-wide view with time ranges (day/week/month/90d), agent breakdown, optional team synthesis. |
| `entire dispatch` | "Generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work" — narrative prose summary of what's happened recently, searchable across branches/repos. |

**Output examples:**
- `entire session info <id>` shows: "Status: idle · started 2 hours ago · active 47 minutes ago · tokens 12.3k"
- Sessions display last prompt (truncated): `> "fix the login flow"` 
- Checkpoint explain renders: commit hash, session ID, agent, model, token usage, files touched, and (optionally) an AI summary

---

### 5. **Taglines & "Why This Exists" Framing**

From the README **"Why Entire"** section (line 13-18):

> - **Understand why code changed, not just what** — Transcripts, prompts, files touched, token usage, tool calls, and more are captured alongside every commit.
> - **Rewind and resume from any checkpoint** — Go back to any previous agent session and pick up exactly where you or a coworker left off.
> - **Full context preserved and searchable** — A versioned record of every AI interaction tied to your git history, with nothing lost.
> - **Zero context switching** — Git-native, two-step setup, works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Pi, and more.

**Game narrative energy:** The framing is about **recovery, transparency, and continuity**. Entire is a "save game" system for AI coding—you can always go back, always see why a change happened, always hand off work to a teammate. It's about **capturing intent** alongside implementation.

---

### Key Narrative Takeaways for Your Game

1. **"Checkpoint" is the hero word.** It's a save point in time: code + metadata + transcript + prompts. Players should understand checkpoints as the unit of work recovery.

2. **Sessions are conversations, checkpoints are milestones.** A session can have many checkpoints (each time you commit). The session is the *story*, the checkpoint is the *turning point*.

3. **Transcripts are the memory.** Everything the agent said/did is recorded in the raw transcript. This is what makes work "transparent" and "reviewable."

4. **The workflow is: work → commit → checkpoint (metadata captured) → resume later or explain to teammates.**

5. **"Dispatch" and "recap" are *summaries* of checkpoints**, not first-class data. They're tools for understanding the bigger picture.

6. **No "memory" in the LLM sense** — Entire captures transcripts (the full conversation history), but doesn't attempt to compress or abstract them into a "learned context."

---

Good luck with the game narrative! The real Entire is fundamentally about **making agent work visible, persistent, and recoverable.**

> AGENT

My honest take: **yes, it's worth changing** — but it's a close call, so here's the reasoning rather than just an answer.

The case for changing: your story now centers on **"mission records"** — the ship runs on its records, you recover the records, you rebuild from them. But the tagline says **"agent memory,"** a different word for the same thing, sitting on the *same screen* seconds before the story plays. And the new story foregrounds the **ship's** record (flight paths, system checks, repair logs, pilot commands) more than an *agent's* memory — so "AGENT memory" now reads slightly disconnected from the fiction the player is about to get.

The case for keeping it: the tagline isn't fiction, it's the *pitch*. "Agent memory" names the real Entire value-prop more directly than "records" does — a passerby gets "oh, this is about AI agents remembering things." Taglines and in-world vocab are allowed to differ.

I lean **change it, to bridge both** — keep the "rebuild your ship" spine (which you liked), but swap "agent memory" for the record concept so the title screen speaks with one voice. Options:

- **REBUILD YOUR SHIP FROM ITS RECORDS** — tightest tie to the new story
- **REBUILD YOUR SHIP FROM THE RECORD IT KEPT** — a hair more voice
- **EVERY FLIGHT LEAVES A RECORD — REBUILD FROM IT** — leads with the idea, more arcade
- **REBUILD YOUR SHIP FROM ITS MISSION RECORDS** — uses the exact story phrase

If you'd rather keep the explicit Entire hook, the minimal move is **REBUILD YOUR SPACESHIP WITH AGENT MEMORY → REBUILD YOUR SHIP FROM ITS AGENT RECORD** — keeps "agent," swaps "memory" for "record" so at least the *noun* matches the story.

My pick: **REBUILD YOUR SHIP FROM ITS RECORDS** — clean, matches the story's lead word, still obviously about recovering the work history. Want that one, a tweak, or to keep "agent memory" as the deliberate product-pitch exception?

**Records (shoot these)** — these are the ship's mission data, so they should look *alive and friendly*, in the planet's palette:

**Crap (let it fall / don't shoot)** — dead stuff, the opposite on every channel:
- **Color:** cold, dull grey/charcoal, scorched. No glow.
- **Shape:** jagged, broken — busted hull plating, asteroid chunks, twisted scrap.
- **Motion:** tumbling erratically, falling faster/heavier.

So the rule the player internalizes in two seconds: **glowing + clean + gold = catch it. Dark + broken + tumbling = junk.**

> AGENT

Got them rendering. And this is exactly why it was worth *seeing* instead of me describing — the screenshot just settled the whole question honestly:

**What works:**
- **Key** — instantly a key. Bow + shaft + teeth reads from across the room. Keep it, no notes.
- **Wreckage vs. records** — the core read is *excellent*. Glowing gold vs. dark jagged debris: you will never confuse "catch" from "skip." That's the most important thing and it's nailed.
- **Wrench** — reads as a tool, though at this angle it's a touch cross/hammer-like. Fixable with a clearer open jaw.

**What fails — and it's instructive:**
- **Compass and gauge are both just gold coins.** Their identifying feature (the needle / the dial face) is *on the flat face*, and the moment the object tilts, that face hides and you get a featureless disc. Worse, they're indistinguishable from *each other*.

And here's the real problem for *this specific game*: these things are **falling and tumbling.** A compass that only reads when it's face-on will be an unidentifiable coin for half of every spin. So **face-dependent instruments (compass, gauge) are a bad fit for a falling-shooter** — while **silhouette-driven ones (key, wrench) read from almost any angle.**

So my honest recommendation shifts: **lean into silhouette objects, drop the disc-faced ones.** A stronger four might be:
- **Key** ✅ (pilot commands / access)
- **Wrench** ✅ (repair logs) — with a cleaner jaw
- **Telescope/spyglass** — a tapered cylinder, reads from any angle (navigation/flight paths, replacing the compass)
- **Antenna or fuel canister** — strong profile (system checks)

Two paths from here — your call:
1. I **swap compass/gauge** for silhouette-strong objects (telescope, etc.) and re-render the set, or
2. I **keep compass/gauge but force them face-on** with a huge bright needle (works, but fights the tumbling).

I'd go with **#1**. Want me to re-roll the lineup that way?

(Temp mockup files are untracked — I'll delete them when we're done.)

Right — whether this shooter **replaces the island level or becomes its own place.** Here's the fuller picture, because it changes how it ties into the fiction and the existing flow.

The flow you have now is: **orbit → click the landing site → land → Level 1 (walk the island).** The shooter has to slot into that without breaking it. Two ways:

**A) Same location, new gameplay — the crash site.**
You still click the landing site and drop in, but instead of walking the island, you're standing *at your crash site* on the surface. The island stays as the backdrop (sky, terrain, your downed ship), and the records rain **down out of the sky over the wreck** — the "scattered records" being pulled back toward you. Your ship's cannon is mounted at the crash site, pointing up. You shoot the falling records, bank them per wave.
- *Pros:* reuses all the island art, keeps the orbit→land→Level 1 flow intact, and "recover what scattered" reads perfectly.
- *Cons:* it's a full rewrite of `islandView.js`'s gameplay (but the *stage* survives).

**B) New location — the descent / debris field.**
The shooter is the **fall itself**, between orbit and the surface. After you pick the landing site, you plunge through the upper atmosphere and your scattered records + wreckage are tumbling through the air around you. You shoot them on the way down. Then you land. The island could stay as a *separate* later beat (or get repurposed).
- *Pros:* gives the descent real gameplay (right now it's just a crossfade), and a sky/debris-field is a natural home for "falling from the sky."
- *Cons:* it's a brand-new scene to build from scratch, and it adds a step to the flow.

**My pick: A.** It's less to build, keeps everything you already like, and the "records raining back down on your crash site, blast them out of the wreckage" image is strong and on-fiction. B is cooler in theory but it's a whole new scene and an extra step for not much more payoff.

Either way the orbit title/story flow you just polished stays untouched — this only changes what happens *after* you land.

Which location feels right — recover-at-the-crash-site (A), or shoot-on-the-way-down (B)?

Forget build cost — noted, that's my problem not yours. Let me answer the actual question: **where is the player standing.**

**Option A — yes, still on the planet.** You've landed. You're on the surface, at your crash site, looking up. Your downed ship and the island terrain are right there around you. The records rain down out of the sky and you shoot *up* at them from the ground. You never leave the planet — the whole game stays "I crashed here, I'm fixing my ship here." That's one consistent place from landing to liftoff.

**Option B — no, you're in the air.** The shooter happens *during the fall*, before you touch down. You're in the sky/atmosphere, not on the planet yet — you land *after* the shooting. So there'd be a stretch where you're not actually on the planet.

Given your instinct, **A is the one that keeps the player grounded on the planet** — which I think is right, because the fiction is "you crashed *on this planet*, the records scattered *across this planet*, fix your ship." Staying at the crash site the whole time makes the place feel real and continuous.

The one thing A needs is a reason the records are *falling from the sky* if you're already on the ground. Cleanest answer: **the crash flung them skyward and they're still raining back down over the wreck** — you blast them out of the air to recover them before they smash into the ground and break further. That gives you both "on the planet" *and* "falling from the sky" without contradiction.

So: you're at your ship, on the planet, shooting falling records out of the sky. That the picture you want?

45	  { x: 28, z: 38 },
46	  { x: -30, z: 36 },
47	];
48	const DEV_LEVEL2_CHECKPOINTS = ["31f0cafe4d12", "7e11a2b09c44", "b0a7ded51a6e"];

50	// What the terminal asks for at each stage of a memory's recovery.
51	const STEPS = {
52	  dormant:   { type: "command", cmd: "git add",    accept: ["git add"],    hint: "Stage the recovered memory" },
53	  recovered: { type: "command", cmd: "git commit", accept: ["git commit"], hint: "Commit it before the clock runs out" },
54	  frozen:    { type: "confirm", question: "Link this commit to a checkpoint?",
55	               hint: "Entire offers to capture the session behind this commit" },
56	};
57	// After every memory is linked, the player reviews them with this command.
58	const REVIEW_STEP = {
59	  type: "command", cmd: "entire checkpoint list", accept: ["entire checkpoint list"],
60	  hint: "All memories recovered — review what you've banked",
61	};
62	
63	function normalizeCmd(s) {
64	  return s.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, " ");
65	}
66	function cmdMatches(input, accepts) {
67	  const n = normalizeCmd(input);
68	  return accepts.some((a) => n === a || n.startsWith(a + " "));
69	}

71	export function createIslandView(renderer, { onExit, onComplete, onNext, devStartLevel = 1 } = {}) {
72	  const canvas = renderer.domElement;
73	  const devLevel2 = devStartLevel === 2;
74	
75	  // ---------- scene & sky ----------
76	  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
77	  scene.background = new THREE.Color(0x2a2350); // lavender dusk sky
78	  scene.fog = new THREE.Fog(0x2a2350, 90, 320);

81	    62, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 2000
82	  );
83	
84	  // ---------- lighting (soft, warm sun in a lavender sky) ----------
85	  scene.add(new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xcdbcff, 0x3a2f5e, 0.7));

89	  scene.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0x6a5a92, 0.3));

91	  const dome = new THREE.Mesh(
92	    new THREE.SphereGeometry(900, 32, 16),
93	    new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x3a3168, side: THREE.BackSide, fog: false })
94	  );
95	  scene.add(dome);
96	
97	  // ---------- terrain ----------
98	  const terrain = createTerrain({ size: 200, segments: 220, maxHeight: 26, seed: 1337 });
99	  scene.add(terrain.mesh, terrain.water);
100	
101	  // ---------- memories ----------
102	  const beamTex = makeBeamTexture();
103	  const artifacts = [];
104	  FRAGMENTS.slice(0, MEMORY_COUNT).forEach((frag, idx) => {
105	    const place = PLACEMENTS[idx % PLACEMENTS.length];
106	    const groundY = terrain.heightAt(place.x, place.z);
107	    const anchor = new THREE.Group();
108	    anchor.position.set(place.x, groundY, place.z);
109	
110	    const model = BUILDERS[frag.kind]();
111	    model.scale.setScalar(14);
112	    model.position.y = 1.4;
113	    anchor.add(model);
114	
115	    // A tall light beam so the memory is findable from across the island.
116	    const beam = new THREE.Mesh(
117	      new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.6, 0.6, 60, 12, 1, true),
118	      new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({
119	        map: beamTex, color: BEAM_COLOR, transparent: true, opacity: 0.5,
120	        blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending, depthWrite: false, side: THREE.DoubleSide,
121	        fog: false,
122	      })
123	    );
124	    beam.position.y = 30;
125	    anchor.add(beam);
126	
127	    const glow = new THREE.PointLight(BEAM_COLOR, 8, 40, 2);
128	    glow.position.y = 3;
129	    anchor.add(glow);
130	
131	    scene.add(anchor);
132	    artifacts.push({
133	      anchor, model, beam, glow, fragment: frag,
134	      state: "dormant",   // dormant → recovered (staged) → frozen (committed) → checkpointed
135	      ice: null, idSprite: null, core: null, id: null, iceY: 0,
136	      melting: false, meltT: 0,   // melt-away animation when the level times out
137	      bobOff: Math.random() * 10,
138	    });
139	  });
140	
141	  // ---------- first-person controller ----------
142	  const fp = createFirstPerson(camera, canvas, {
143	    heightAt: terrain.heightAt,
144	    radius: terrain.radius * 0.96,
145	    eyeHeight: 2.6,
146	    speed: 24,
147	  });
148	  scene.add(fp.controls.object);
149	
150	  // Bird's-eye map (M) — spot the memory beams from above, keep walking.
151	  const overhead = createOverhead(scene, terrain, camera);
152	  function setMap(on) {
153	    if (overhead.on === on) return;
154	    overhead.set(on);
155	    fp.setAlwaysMove(on);                       // arrows work without pointer lock
156	    scene.fog.near = on ? 500 : 90;             // don't fog the map out
157	    scene.fog.far = on ? 1400 : 320;
158	    crosshair?.classList.toggle("hidden", on || !fp.isLocked);
159	  }
160	
161	  // ---------- HUD elements ----------
162	  const promptEl = document.getElementById("fp-prompt");
163	  const controlsEl = document.getElementById("fp-controls");
164	  const crosshair = document.getElementById("crosshair");
165	  const islandHud = document.getElementById("island-hud");
166	  const tutorialEl = document.getElementById("tutorial");
167	  const actionBar = document.getElementById("action-bar");
168	  const actionBarFill = document.getElementById("action-bar-fill");
169	  const shipMeter = document.getElementById("ship-meter");
170	  const shipMeterFill = document.getElementById("ship-meter-fill");
171	  const shipMeterPct = document.getElementById("ship-meter-pct");
172	  const ckptCard = document.getElementById("ckpt-card");

177	  const termEl = document.getElementById("terminal");
178	  const termHint = document.getElementById("term-hint");
179	  const termInput = document.getElementById("term-input");
180	  const termList = document.getElementById("term-list");
181	  const termMsg = document.getElementById("term-msg");
182	  const termCta = document.getElementById("term-cta");
183	  const countdownEl = document.getElementById("countdown");

185	  const levelFail = document.getElementById("level-fail");

188	  const devLevelBadge = document.getElementById("dev-level-badge");
189	  const fpShared = document.getElementById("fp-shared");
190	
191	  let target = null;            // nearest memory in range
192	  let active = false;           // is this view being shown?
193	  let promptText = null;
194	  let controlsLocked = null;
195	  const taught = new Set();

197	  let cardTimer = null;
198	  let msgTimer = null;

200	  // Terminal state
201	  let terminalOpen = false;
202	  let termTarget = null;        // the memory whose terminal is open
203	  let buffer = "";              // what the player has typed
204	  let dismissedMemory = null;   // memory the player Esc'd out of (until they leave)
205	  let reviewMode = false;       // all linked → review with `entire checkpoint list`
206	  let listShown = false;        // the list has been printed

208	  // Level countdown — the single source of pressure for the whole run.
209	  let timeLeft = TOTAL_TIME;

211	  let failed = false;

213	
214	  const checkpointedCount = () =>
215	    artifacts.filter((a) => a.state === "checkpointed").length;
216	  const allLinked = () => checkpointedCount() >= artifacts.length;
217	
218	  // ---------- HUD helpers ----------
219	  function setPrompt(text) {
220	    if (!promptEl || text === promptText) return;
221	    promptText = text;
222	    if (text) { promptEl.textContent = text; promptEl.classList.remove("hidden"); }
223	    else promptEl.classList.add("hidden");
224	  }
225	  function hideActionBar() { actionBar.classList.add("hidden"); }
226	
227	  // ---------- level countdown ----------
228	  function fmtTime(s) {
229	    s = Math.max(0, Math.ceil(s));
230	    return `${Math.floor(s / 60)}:${String(s % 60).padStart(2, "0")}`;
231	  }
232	  function updateClock() {
233	    if (countdownTime) countdownTime.textContent = fmtTime(timeLeft);
234	    countdownEl?.classList.toggle("is-low", timerRunning && timeLeft <= LOW_TIME);
235	    countdownEl?.classList.toggle("is-critical", timerRunning && timeLeft <= CRIT_TIME);
236	  }
237	
238	  // How hard the sky is panicking right now: 0 = calm lavender, 1 = full crimson throb.
239	  function panicFactor() {
240	    if (failed) return 1;                         // hold the dread behind the fail screen
241	    if (!timerRunning || timeLeft > PANIC_TIME) return 0;
242	    let p = (PANIC_TIME - timeLeft) / PANIC_TIME; // 0 at PANIC_TIME → 1 at 0:00
243	    p *= p;                                        // eased: barely there early, harsh late
244	    if (timeLeft <= CRIT_TIME) {                   // throb once it's critical
245	      const throb = 0.5 + 0.5 * Math.sin(performance.now() / 85);
246	      p += 0.14 * throb;
247	    }
248	    return Math.min(1, p);
249	  }
250	  function applyPanicSky() {
251	    const p = panicFactor();
252	    scene.background.copy(SKY_CALM).lerp(SKY_PANIC, p);
253	    scene.fog.color.copy(SKY_CALM).lerp(FOG_PANIC, p);
254	    dome.material.color.copy(DOME_CALM).lerp(DOME_PANIC, p);
255	    sun.color.copy(SUN_CALM).lerp(SUN_PANIC, p * 0.85);
256	  }
257	  function failLevel() {
258	    if (failed) return;
259	    failed = true;
260	    timerRunning = false;
261	    setMap(false);
262	    closeTerminal(false);
263	    fp.detach();                  // freeze the player behind the fail screen
264	    // Un-banked memories always melt; if they ran out the clock on the final
265	    // `entire checkpoint list` (all banked, not yet reviewed), the whole run melts.
266	    for (const a of artifacts) {
267	      if (reviewMode || a.state !== "checkpointed") { a.melting = true; a.meltT = MELT_DUR; }
268	    }
269	    countdownEl?.classList.remove("is-low", "is-critical");
270	    tutorialEl?.classList.add("hidden");
271	    levelFail?.classList.remove("hidden");
272	  }
273	  function resetLevel() {
274	    failed = false;
275	    levelFail?.classList.add("hidden");
276	    if (active) fp.attach();      // movement resumes for the new run
277	    for (const a of artifacts) {
278	      if (a.ice) { a.anchor.remove(a.ice); a.ice = null; }
279	      if (a.idSprite) { a.anchor.remove(a.idSprite); a.idSprite = null; }
280	      if (a.core) { a.anchor.remove(a.core); a.core = null; }
281	      a.state = "dormant";
282	      a.id = null;
283	      a.melting = false; a.meltT = 0;
284	      a.model.position.y = 1.4;
285	      setModelOpacity(a.model, 1);
286	    }
287	    reviewMode = false;
288	    listShown = false;
289	    dismissedMemory = null;
290	    shipMeter?.classList.remove("is-full");
291	    setPower();
292	    timeLeft = TOTAL_TIME;
293	    timerRunning = true;
294	    updateClock();
295	    showTutorial("New attempt — bank all three memories before the clock hits zero.", 4500);
296	  }

298	  // Dev-only Level 2 entry point: pretend Level 1 has already been completed so
299	  // the next level can be built/tested without replaying the timed tutorial.
300	  function seedLevel2DevState() {
301	    started = true;
302	    failed = false;
303	    timerRunning = false;
304	    reviewMode = false;
305	    listShown = true;
306	    dismissedMemory = null;
307	    levelFail?.classList.add("hidden");
308	    briefingEl?.classList.add("hidden");
309	    termEl?.classList.add("hidden");
310	
311	    artifacts.forEach((a, idx) => {
312	      a.state = "checkpointed";
313	      a.id = DEV_LEVEL2_CHECKPOINTS[idx % DEV_LEVEL2_CHECKPOINTS.length];
314	      a.melting = false;
315	      a.meltT = 0;

318	
319	      if (!a.ice) {
320	        const ice = makeIceBlock();

322	        a.iceY = ice.position.y;
323	        a.anchor.add(ice);
324	        a.ice = ice;
325	      }
326	      a.ice.material.opacity = 0.62;
327	      a.ice.material.emissive.setHex(0x2a6c8a);
328	      a.ice.material.emissiveIntensity = 1.1;
329	
330	      if (!a.core) {
331	        const core = new THREE.PointLight(0x8fe3ff, 6, 26, 2);
332	        core.position.copy(a.ice.position);
333	        a.anchor.add(core);
334	        a.core = core;
335	      }
336	      if (!a.idSprite) {
337	        const spr = makeIdSprite(a.id);
338	        spr.position.y = a.iceY + 5;
339	        a.anchor.add(spr);
340	        a.idSprite = spr;
341	      }
342	
343	      a.beam.visible = false;
344	      a.glow.visible = false;

350	    applyPanicSky();
351	  }

353	  // Landing briefing — the level is frozen (no clock, no movement) until START.
354	  function showBriefing() {

358	    briefingEl?.classList.remove("hidden");

361	    if (started) return;

369	  }
370	  briefingStartBtn?.addEventListener("click", startLevel);

372	  function showTutorial(text, ms = 5500) {

378	  }
379	  function teachOnce(key, text, ms) {

382	    showTutorial(text, ms);
383	  }
384	
385	  function setPower() {
386	    const pct = Math.round((checkpointedCount() / artifacts.length) * 100);
387	    // Vertical gauge — fills bottom-up and shifts color as memory is restored.
388	    if (shipMeterFill) shipMeterFill.style.height = pct + "%";
389	    if (shipMeterPct) shipMeterPct.textContent = pct + "%";
390	    if (shipMeter) {

392	      shipMeter.classList.toggle("lvl-mid", pct > 34 && pct < 100);
393	      shipMeter.classList.toggle("lvl-high", pct >= 100);
394	    }
395	  }
396	  function showCard(a, shipPct) {

400	    ccAttrFill.style.width = shipPct + "%";

402	    ckptCard.classList.remove("hidden");
